transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-02-11
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~60 minutes
- Attendees: Avery Chen, Miguel Soto (Redwood); Priya Narang, Darren Li, Sana Patel (Borealis AI)

Summary:
Redwood SE and AE led a deep technical triage with Borealis AI focused on intermittent latency spikes and quality regressions correlated with KV cache evictions during long-context replays. Topics covered: eviction jitter causes, paging behavior under heavy prefix reuse, impact of int8/int4 quantization on cache residency and KV lookup cost, batching trade-offs, and VPC/on-prem telemetry access for isolated repros.

Topics mentioned:
- KV eviction patterns and jitter
- Long-context replay (session stitching)
- Prefix reuse hotspots and eviction churn
- Quantization sensitivity (accuracy vs memory)
- Batching/cold KV lookups and tail latency
- Telemetry needed for root cause

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone thanks for taking the time, um we're gonna dig in to the eviction jitter that you reported last week. we got the initial traces from your team, thanks priya. can you kick us off with the user impact?
[00:15] Priya: sure, so basically every few hours we see a cluster of 200-300ms p95 spikes, sometimes p99 hits like 800ms, those line up with long conversation replays where the prompt length balloons and we suspect k v spill or paging. it's intermittent, not consistent.
[00:30] Darren: and to add, it's most pronounced on our cohort that uses context stitching across 20+ turns, so prefix reuse is high.
[00:45] Miguel: when you say prefix reuse, do you mean identical prefix tokens across sessions or similar semantic prefixes?
[00:50] Priya: mostly identical system+user tokens — e.g., standardized case templates. so the same keys are getting hot.
[00:58] Miguel: got it. that usually increases the chance of hot-prefix eviction thrashing if the tokenstore is capacity-constrained.
[01:10] Sana: quick note, we run the model on a quantized int8 footprint in staging — we recently tested int4 in one branch — could that affect eviction frequency?
[01:22] Miguel: yes, quantization changes memory density, which can increase effective residency pressure, but it also changes kernel latencies. int4 may cause more cacheline misalignments in our runtime's KV layout. i've seen scenarios where int4 reduces model memory but forces more frequent kv layering and spill.
[01:40] Priya: so switching to int4 could be the trigger for the jitter? we rolled that out last month.
[01:47] Avery: maybe — though it's usually a combination: quantization adjusts footprint, traffic patterns hit a hot-prefix, and batching interplay leads to intermittent spikes. we'll need to correlate timestamps across metrics.
[02:00] Miguel: one more datapoint — the traces you sent show a sudden jump in network IO around the p99 events; that suggests spill/paging to disk or remote KV node rather than pure CPU. do you have node-level disk metrics?
[02:15] Darren: yes we have io stats, but they're aggregated; we can pull per-pod disk latency. we'll share.
[02:22] Miguel: for root cause, the thing i want to test is eviction jitter vs steady-state eviction: introduce controlled prefix storms in staging and observe whether eviction events align with the jitter. we'll also toggle batch sizes — small batches show higher idle lookups, bigger batches increase queueing but amortize KV calls.
[02:40] Priya: what's the behavior if the cache evicts while the model still tries to use the kv cache? do we block on fetch?
[02:46] Miguel: the runtime has two modes: blocking fetch (sync) and async prefetch. by default we use blocking to guarantee correctness which can add tail latency if remote kv is slow. we can switch to async prefetch for certain routes but need to accept some staleness risk.
[03:05] Avery: staleness is a product decision — for your use case with templated prefixes, async prefetch might be acceptable since the prefixes are deterministic, but for personalized slots it's risky.
[03:20] Darren: we also saw increased thundering herd when many requests re-warm the same prefix after eviction. is there a built-in backoff?
[03:27] Miguel: yes, we have exponential jitter on re-warm requests and a request coalescing mechanism. but when the hot-prefix is evicted across many shards simultaneously (e.g., during a memory compaction), coalescing can't prevent all contention.
[03:45] Priya: what's your recommendation operationally? we want minimal p99 impact without moving to dedicated capacity yet.
[03:52] Miguel: short term: increase tokenstore ttl for hot prefixes, widen your hot-prefix bucket so more capacity for re-use, and tune prefetch thresholds so we prefetch on warmups rather than after eviction. medium term: run targeted eviction jitter benchmarks with different quantization configs to see memory vs eviction trade-offs.
[04:10] Sana: can you describe the benchmark? we want to reproduce reliably before we change prod.
[04:15] Miguel: we'll create a synthetic workload that replays your prefix distribution at scaled QPS, vary model quantization (fp16, int8, int4), vary batching window (8ms, 30ms, 100ms), and track eviction frequency, p95/p99 latency, and remote io. we'll also instrument KV hit/miss histograms by prefix.
[04:40] Priya: ok, we'll provide the prefix distribution file.
[04:43] Miguel: perfect. also, we need to look at your slab allocation — if slab sizes are small, int4 compaction may squeeze more prefixes into fewer slabs causing cross-prefix eviction when one big prefix expands.
[04:58] Darren: are slabs per-shard or global?
[05:02] Miguel: per-shard. your shard map shows some skew — a few shards have higher resident set sizes. that can create local hotspots and lead to cross-shard remote fetches.
[05:15] Priya: skew could be due to key hashing changes after a rolling update or our routing policy change. we recently changed routing to route by user region.
[05:25] Miguel: that matters — routing-affinity changes can re-concentrate prefixes. worth checking the routing map at the time of spikes.
[05:35] Avery: let's capture the mapping at spike times; that will tell us if a redistribution correlated with the first int4 rollout.
[05:45] Sana: side question — for on-prem, what telemetry access do you need? we are constrained about uploading traces externally.
[05:52] Miguel: we can run the profiler sandbox within your VPC if you install our collector; alternatively you can run Redwood's profiling container offline and share sanitized artifacts. ideally we want per-process KV eviction logs, slab occupancy, and per-prefix hit/miss rates. if that's not possible, sanitized histograms work too.
[06:12] Priya: we can run the collector inside our staging cluster. we prefer not to run external binaries in prod.
[06:18] Miguel: that's fine; staging is sufficient for repros. we'll provide the container image and a runbook for minimal permissions.
[06:24] Priya: great.
[06:30] Miguel: another angle is batching and latency — when you increase batch windows to reduce compute cost, KV calls get concentrated in spikes, which can cause transient IO pressure. at the extremes, it looks like evictions triggered by big batches.
[06:44] Darren: hmm, we have been increasing batching to save on token cost. maybe that backfired during high concurrency.
[06:50] Avery: tradeoffs. we should test batching x quantization combos. Miguel, can you produce a matrix?
[06:56] Miguel: yes — i'll do a 3x3 grid: batch window (8/30/100ms) x quant (fp16/int8/int4) and capture evictions, p95/p99, and cost.
[07:08] Priya: how about prefix reuse mitigation — can the runtime shard hot prefixes differently without redeploy?
[07:15] Miguel: we have a hot-prefix replication mode that increases replica count for top-K prefixes, but that requires reserved capacity since it increases memory usage. it's a middle ground between dedicated and hosted.
[07:28] Priya: can that be enabled for only select routes?
[07:32] Miguel: yes, route-level policy works — you can opt-in specific API keys or model routes.
[07:38] Sana: will that solve the thundering herd?
[07:41] Miguel: it reduces remote fetches because more replicas hold the hot prefix locally, but if eviction happens at all replicas you'll still see some tail. replication plus staggered ttl renewal helps.
[07:54] Darren: what about flush/compaction cycles — could those be the cause for synchronized evictions?
[08:00] Miguel: yes, compaction can cause synchronized frees. compaction policies are typically staggered but under certain memory pressure compaction is accelerated and happens cluster-wide. we can add stagger jitter to compaction in your staging runtime.
[08:15] Priya: that sounds promising.
[08:20] Miguel: last note on quantization: int4 sometimes triggers different kernel paths where KV load instruction timings differ. that can amplify tail latencies if combined with remote IO. so while int4 reduces memory and nominal cost, it can create non-linear tail behavior.
[08:40] Priya: so we should probably roll back int4 in prod until we finish the benchmarks?
[08:45] Avery: that's a conservative choice. alternatively, toggle int4 only on a small canary with strict observability.
[08:55] Priya: we'll canary it.
[08:58] Miguel: i'll also instrument more aggressive coalescing for your routes in staging so we can compare.
[09:05] Sana: on the topic of instrumentation, what exact traces do you need?
[09:09] Miguel: per-request KV timeline (local lookup start/end, remote fetch start/end), slab occupancy time-series, eviction events with reason codes, and per-prefix access counts. also, kernel-level cpu samples around p99 events help.
[09:28] Priya: we can capture all that in staging. we'll share a sanitized bundle.
[09:32] Avery: excellent. next steps recap — Miguel runs the eviction jitter matrix, Priya will share prefix distribution and staging access, Sana will run p99 trace captures, Darren will extract disk IO histograms. we'll re-sync next week.
[09:48] Priya: one more question on toolchain: if we go for dedicated capacity later, how straightforward is migrating the shard map and preserving cache warmness?
[09:57] Miguel: we have a warm migration tool — it streams prefix snapshots into the new capacity, and we support phased cutover, but it takes time and network bandwidth. preserving warmness across a big tenant can take hours unless you pre-warm with replay.
[10:14] Priya: ok that's helpful.
[10:20] Darren: can you share an estimated cost delta for hot-prefix replication vs reserved capacity?
[10:24] Avery: we'll send a ballpark in the follow-up doc — replication costs are roughly proportional to memory footprint of top-K prefixes plus a small management surcharge.
[10:34] Miguel: one final note — sometimes third-party infra changes (like kernel updates, cgroups changes) affect IO latencies; check your node kernel logs around the first int4 rollout timestamp.
[10:47] Priya: good call, we'll check.
[10:52] Avery: ok, thank you all. we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and the runner container. any last minute?
[10:59] Sana: no, thanks — appreciate the specific asks.
[11:02] Miguel: thanks everyone, we'll get started.
